title: Insurers dodge Microsoft chaos
full_text:
Millions of workers were locked out of Microsoft’s flagship software for more than a day last week, stalling everything from doctors’ offices to corporate earnings calls. But insurers have breathed a sigh of relief.
Despite triggering global panic widespread disruption, the Microsoft 365 outage is projected to cost the cyber insurance market next to nothing.
Reinsurance broker Marsh Re said the widespread chaos did not automatically result in material insurance losses. Morningstar estimates losses to be between $US300m ($442.64m) and $US500m, globally.
“So far, this appears to be a significant but uneven disruption with broad geographic exposure and progressive recovery, not a complete Microsoft 365 outage, a cloud infrastructure failure, or a cyberattack,” Marsh wrote in a report about the outage. “The impact on the insurance market is expected to be minimal, given the uneven nature of the disruption and likelihood that most losses will be limited to short-term productivity and operational delays.” The outage began about 3am on Friday. Microsoft apologised to customers and restored services on Saturday morning, vowing to release its review into the meltdown once it is completed. It blamed a faulty upgrade, which crippled its servers, and ruled out a cyber attack or rogue artificial intelligence-powered agents.
“We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers,” Microsoft executive vice-president of Copilot, agents, and platform Charles Lamanna said. “We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it. I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity.” During the outage, Australia’s biggest hospitals could not communicate with patients via email, instead directing them to phone clinicians. Telstra’s emails were also frozen. ANZ advised its customers to look out for potential scams, following the shutdown, while ASIO and the Australian Federal Police were also hit.
But while cyber policies typically respond to business interruptions and contingent losses, payouts depend heavily on strict qualifying thresholds.
This includes policy waiting periods that average four hours for smaller organisations and 12 hours or more for larger ones, alongside the requirement to prove an actual loss of profit.
“For cover to be triggered, affected organisations must not only experience disruption beyond the applicable waiting period, but also demonstrate an actual loss of profit,” Marsh said.
“In this instance, we believe the proportion of revenue, and therefore profit, affected is likely to be minimal.
“This is largely due to the nature of the disrupted services, as the loss of access to email services is expected to have limited financial impact on most sectors and organisations.” But Marsh said the outage highlighted the global reach of widely used Microsoft services and the potential for a service disruption to affect organisations across multiple regions and sectors.
“It also provides a useful example of how a high-profile technology incident can involve partial degradation and staggered recovery without resulting in a complete interruption for all users.” Morningstar vice-president of European Financial Institutions Mario de Cicco also expected limited insurance losses.
“The Microsoft outage could result in a number of insurance claims, mostly related to businesses experiencing financial losses, operational disruptions, and delays in serving customers. However, not all businesses will automatically be entitled to compensation, as this depends on the terms and conditions of their insurance policies,” Mr Cicco said.
“Some cyber insurance policies only cover losses caused by malicious cyberattacks, whereas the Microsoft outage appears to have resulted from a technical failure rather than a deliberate attack. Additionally, some policies include waiting periods before business interruption cover becomes effective.” Council of Small Business Organisations Australia chief executive Sky Cappuccio said the outage caused “significant disruption” and will “inevitably have a productivity impact”. “For many office-based businesses, the loss of access to core systems, emails and other digital tools has meant being unable to perform many day-to-day tasks,” Ms Cappuccio said.
